profile.story: Anil Patel has run Summit Peak IT out of Denver since 2014 — 61 managed clients, 1,480 seats, sixteen people. Eighty percent of revenue is contracted and recurring, logo retention is 96%, and the company closes its books inside fifteen days into a board pack it actually reads. This is the healthy case: the machine works. What is left is a set of small, specific gaps — 40% of the seat base still priced on pre-2025 agreements, a security attach rate stuck at 34%, and 9.2 hours a week of after-hours tier-1 triage that two engineers rotate a pager for. Anil is 51 and has put a partial recapitalisation on the objective list, which is why module E is in scope.

intake.q2: We are a managed service provider. Sixty-one clients between 15 and 210 seats — professional services, healthcare practices, credit unions, a few light manufacturers — on per-seat monthly agreements that cover the service desk, endpoint management, patching, backup and a quarterly technology review. On top of that we sell security add-ons, backup and DR as a service, co-managed support for clients who have their own IT person, and project work: migrations, refreshes, office moves. Everything is delivered remotely from Denver with a field engineer on the road three days a week.

blockNotes.b1: Anil is the rare owner who did not name one bottleneck — he named four small ones and said he could not sequence them. That is an accurate read of his own business and the session should say so rather than manufacture a crisis. Objective is Prepare to scale with a partial exit in 4–5 years, so module E is in scope. Seventeen days away last year with no calls.
blockNotes.b2: Front end is genuinely good. Eighteen inquiries a month, every one in HubSpot, sub-fifteen-minute callback on the scorecard, five stages actually used, 52% close on qualified opportunities. Funnel reconciles: 24 qualified opportunities a year × 52% × $34,200 first-year recurring = ~$427K of new ARR against 96% logo retention on a $3.1M base — lands on the P&L's 10% growth. Pass.
blockNotes.b3: Systems tour ran long because there was a lot to see. HubSpot↔ConnectWise↔QuickBooks↔BrightGauge all connected and shown moving data. Two double-entry points survive: the monthly seat reconciliation before invoicing, and a project spreadsheet running alongside ConnectWise that Devon admits should have died two years ago. IT Glue SOP library opened at random — four of five entries current.
blockNotes.b4: 19.3 h/wk of repetitive work across sixteen people (~630 available hours) — 3%, pass. 9.2 of those hours are after-hours tier-1 triage on a rotating pager, which is both the largest task and the source of the only real resistance in the company (q59).
blockNotes.b5: Continuity is in better shape than most companies twice this size: written agreements, current insurance, IP owned, a continuity plan drafted. The finding is the one Anil raised himself in e6 — 61 auto-renewing agreements and no lawyer has ever read one for change-of-control. Recorded as a nontransferable-contracts watch and an attorney referral, not as advice. Second finding worth printing: q48 flags unclear ownership on the company's own marketing and domain accounts, and the Microsoft partner portal is under Anil's personal login. They secure their clients better than themselves.

assessment.owner_objective: Prepare to scale toward $5M with a partial recapitalisation in four to five years — and get new-logo acquisition out of the owner's calendar before that conversation starts.
assessment.owner_belief: Honestly I do not think we have one big bottleneck — I think we have four small ones and I cannot tell which to do first. If you pushed me I would say sales: every new logo still closes because I am in the room, and that is the thing that will cap us at five million.
assessment.primary_constraint: New-logo acquisition is the one process in the company that has never been systematised: every other workflow is documented, owned, measured and automated, and this one runs on the founder being in the room — which caps growth at his calendar and is the single item a partial-sale buyer will price down.
assessment.constraint_symptoms: Block 1: 'every new logo still closes because I am in the room', and q4 sets the target at six a year without him. Block 2: the seven-touch sequence covers inbound and stops at partner introductions — the highest-quality source at 7 a month — because those are Anil's. Block 3: the sales workflow is the one of ten with the thinnest SOP entry in an otherwise current library. Block 5: q52 puts new-logo acquisition first on the key-person list, and e6 ties the exit itself to whether the base is transferable without him. Four blocks; the rule requires two.
assessment.constraint_cost: ~$137K of first-year recurring revenue a year not pursued because qualified opportunities queue behind one calendar (24 qualified/yr against 18 inquiries/mo, funnel Doc) · ~$61K of contribution sitting in the 26-point gap between a 34% security attach rate and the 60% target on a 1,480-seat base · 0 new logos closed without the owner in three years, against a stated target of six.
assessment.constraint_fix: Write the sales workflow the way the other nine are written: a qualification standard, a discovery script, cost-backed pricing floors the account managers can hold without escalation, and partner introductions routed into the same sequence as everything else. Give Jaycee and Ben one segment each to own end to end, and measure new logos closed without Anil as a weekly KPI beside the other six.
assessment.momentum_initiative: Reprice the seat base still on pre-2025 agreements. It is a decision rather than a project, the January 2026 rate card and the annual review memo already justify it, it touches 40% of the recurring base, and it lands in the P&L inside 60 days.

opportunities.title: Bring the pre-2025 agreements onto the current rate card
opportunities.finding: The January 2026 rate card and the annual price-review memo are both on file and both defensible — priced from per-seat tool cost plus a target engineer load. Roughly 40% of the seat base ($980K of annual recurring revenue) is still billing on agreements written before that review. Logo retention is 96% and net revenue retention 103%, so the base tolerates a price move; nothing has been asked of it.
opportunities.blueprint: Run the pre-2025 agreements in anniversary order, present the current card with the review memo attached, and hold the tier rather than discount to close the gap. Front Range Credit Union goes last and gets a scoped conversation rather than a letter.
opportunities.replaces: Agreements that have auto-renewed at their original per-seat price through two rounds of tool-stack cost increases.

opportunities.title: Close more of the project and vCIO proposals already going out
opportunities.finding: Project proposals to existing clients close at 62% and represent $690K of quoted volume a year. Loss reasons are a free-text note rather than a required field and roughly a third of closed-lost records have it blank, so the company cannot say what it is losing on. The projects line is also the lowest-margin at 41% and the only one that has not moved in two years — because project margin is only known after the project closes.
opportunities.blueprint: Make loss reason a required field on the closed-lost stage, put a real-time margin view on open projects so scope creep is visible before it is billed, and give the account managers option-based proposals rather than a single number. Incremental cost is carried at 8% for the project-engineer overtime the added work will absorb before a hire.
opportunities.replaces: Single-option project proposals, an unenforced loss-reason field, and a project margin nobody sees until the work is finished.

opportunities.title: Automate after-hours tier-1 triage
opportunities.finding: 9.2 h/wk — the single largest task in the repetitive-work inventory — is after-hours tier-1 triage and password resets on a rotating pager. It is the reason the service desk is the one group in the company resisting change (q59), and it is the load standing between the current team and the utilization headroom the growth plan assumes.
opportunities.blueprint: Self-service password reset and MFA re-enrolment through Entra, automated triage and routing on the top six after-hours ticket types, and a documented escalation path for everything else. This is also the change that buys the team's appetite for the rest of the roadmap — fix the pager first and the resistance in q59 goes away.
opportunities.replaces: A rotating after-hours pager absorbing 478 engineer hours a year on tickets that do not need a human.
